stem: Interveinal chlorosis appears only in one irrigation zone. Which differential is strongest?
choices: Treat the localized chlorosis as a micronutrient deficiency because symptoms confined to one irrigation zone are most consistent with uneven nutrient delivery.
Increase the suspected micronutrient only in the affected zone and use the plant response as the main confirmation test.
Prioritize root-zone pH as the cause because a zone-limited pattern is more likely to reflect nutrient availability than foliar or environmental stress.
Keep nutrition, localized delivery/root-zone conditions, and plausible look-alikes in the differential until zone-specific evidence separates them.
rationale: A symptom restricted to one irrigation zone makes localized delivery and root-zone conditions important, but it does not establish a specific nutrient deficiency or pH mechanism. Similar chlorosis can arise from nutrient supply, availability, root impairment, irrigation distribution, environmental effects, or other look-alikes. The strongest workup uses the spatial pattern to prioritize zone-specific evidence while keeping multiple explanations open until discriminating data are collected.
